interactions.summary: Jiang presses the class to name the logical contradiction in Piccarda's contentment, and a student argues that heavenly hierarchy becomes incoherent if obedience means one can neither desire nor intelligibly receive a higher sphere.

Carol reads Piccarda's account of taking the veil, being violently removed from the cloister, and keeping the veil in her heart even after forced return to the world, alongside Costanza's parallel case.

Jiang paraphrases Piccarda and Costanza as women forced out of religious vows for dynastic marriage, then sharpens the paradox by saying the lowest sphere implies divine disapproval even though they appear to have done nothing wrong.

speaker_notes.note: The ASR is noisy in the read-aloud passage, but the stable content is Piccarda's forced removal from the convent and the claim that her inner vow remained intact.
Jiang's phrase about the body and heart being 'chaste' is mistranscribed, but the contrast is clear: outward violation versus inward loyalty to God.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that Piccarda's logic produces a contradiction: if obedience to God's placement is enough for happiness, then a ranked hierarchy of heavenly spheres makes no sense.

The student's answer says advancement inside heaven becomes unintelligible because wanting a higher sphere would already betray the contentment required for the lower one, while being moved upward against one's will would also be incoherent.
Piccarda's speech says she took religious vows as a young woman, was violently removed from her cloister, and nevertheless never loosened the veil in her heart.
Jiang glosses Piccarda's story as aristocratic power politics: her brother needed her as a pawn for alliance-making and forced her into marriage despite her desire to serve God.
Jiang says the lowest sphere itself signals that God does not fully approve of Piccarda and Costanza's outcome, which turns their apparent innocence into a theological paradox.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang states bluntly that heavenly hierarchy 'makes absolutely no sense' if obedience alone explains blessedness.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's hinge from passive summary into a sharper attack on the internal logic of paradise.

signature_moments.moment: Piccarda's vow survives as an inward veil even after the world tears away the outward one.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the veil upon her heart was never loosed
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the class the core image for inner fidelity surviving external coercion.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reduces dynastic politics to a brother using his sister as a pawn.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a pawn for his power politics
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses the violence of aristocratic alliance-making into one memorable causal phrase.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The second woman named alongside Piccarda as another nun forced back into worldly marriage while remaining inwardly attached to her vow.
Dante's image for an inward vow that remains intact even when the visible religious habit is stripped away.
Jiang's frame for the dynastic alliance logic that drags vowed women back out of cloistered life.

chronology_notes.note: This June 15 packet moves from the abstract paradox of heavenly hierarchy into the concrete case of Piccarda and Costanza, using forced marriage as the test case for divine judgment.

uncertainty_notes.note: Several proper names and one chastity contrast are mistranscribed, so extraction keeps only the stable structure of forced vows, marriage, and inward loyalty.
